doc.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, November 11, 2017 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Watching Joe Williams and Miles; apprenticeship and jam sessions
summary: Gates describes learning stage presence by watching Joe Williams and Miles Davis, then argues musicians need apprenticeship like plumbers.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: You know? “Nice try baby, come back another time.” So that’ll either make you quit or go home and work on it. Or you know I went to watch before I ever tried to do this, I was a fan. So I saw Joe Williams sing a lot of times. And I wasn’t just listening to him sing, I would watch the way he would get up from the stool. I mean you do something a little different when you’re on stage, because they realized that yeah you’re listening to me but you’re also looking at me. So you have to present yourself in a certain way. Miles Davis, I want to get back to what we’re talking about but Miles Davis, you know, Miles Davis didn’t do an act, but people came to see what he was going to do next. I wonder what Miles is going to wear? I wonder if he’s going to walk off again. Gee I hope he turns his back on me. You know. I mean what he did made people come to listen and look at him. Because it was interesting. What’s he going to do now? Is he going to talk? I remember watching something where he holds up the band’s members names on a placard. Somebody would solo and he would hold up his placard. Hold it up, put it down. Wow that’s different.
With Kenny Garrett. When Kenny Garrett was playing with him and the cat now, he’s really a great player, a piano player, his name escapes me. MR. Kirkland? Kenny Kirkland?
No. He plays with the famous trio. They’ve been together forever. They play nothing but standards, they never rehearsed. They played great.

Keith Jarrett, yeah. He’d hold up a sign, “Keith Jarrett.” And the audience is going wow. That’s show biz. So I went to see people, and now, I’m not saying that any student should come to see me. That’s not what I’m saying. But I have done gigs in clubs where the last set is a jam session. Not for me. When I’m done then they bring a different rhythm section up and it’s a jam session. In come all the students. Why weren’t you here to catch whatever was happening first? Maybe you could learn something from it. “I’m not interested in that man, I know what I’m doing.” You do? Where’d you learn it? “I go to school.” Oh. How come for everything else that you do there’s an apprenticeship. You can’t just — you don’t go buy a hammer and a saw and you’re a carpenter. You’ve got to be a helper for three years so you learn how to do it.

Plumbers have to learn more than water runs downhill. There’s more to learn than that. You’ve got to be an apprenticeship. You’ve got to carry the tools for everybody first. That doesn’t happen anymore.
